newsitem.title: UK: UK to get first tv debate between party leaders.
newsitem.headline: UK to get first tv debate between party leaders.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major has agreed to a live television debate with opposition Labour leader Tony Blair once an election campaign gets underway. It will be Britain's first such head-to-head between the leaders of the two main political parties.

Conservative Party sources said on Saturday that Major, whose Conservative Party is trailing Labour by more than 20 points in opinion polls, had agreed to the challenge set down by Blair several weeks ago.
Major is shortly expected to call nationwide elections for May 1 and is fighting to regain the initiative for the Conservatives who have been in power for 18 years.

One newspaper report, which could not be confirmed, said Major could announce the election date as early as Monday. Details of the television debate were not released but Blair's office welcomed the prospect, saying it would be an "important contribution" to the election process.

Televised head-to-head debates between leading candidates are common in U.S. presidential elections but have not been tried previously in Britain where parties run their campaigns mainly through public rallies and party broadcasts.
Political sources said Major, 53, often portrayed as the grey man of British politics, agreed to the debate after his advisers told him he had nothing to lose.
Blair, 43, has revamped his party since taking over the leadership in 1994 and appears to be on his way to becoming Britain's youngest prime minister this century. But critics call him "smarmy".

Major's decision came as the the latest opinion poll showed Labour stretching its lead over the Conservatives. The NOP poll for the Sunday Times put Labour on 52 percent, a three point increase over last month, Conservatives down four on 27 percent and Liberal Democrats unchanged on 13 percent.
However 25 percent said they had not definitely made up their minds which way they would vote.
In a keynote speech to Conservatives on Saturday, Major set out his vision of a people's Britain where "everyone can make their own choices and live their own lives."
He insisted that despite the grim news from opinion polls his party would would win a fifth consecutive term of office in "one of the most crucial general elections we have known for generations".
Major said voting for Labour would be like waking up on an airplane whose captain and crew had never flown before, saying "You can only be sure with the Conservatives."
